clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive leukoencephalopathy caused by variants in RNASET2, which encodes a ribonuclease
The MRI pattern closely mimics congenital cytomegalovirus infection, with multifocal patchy white matter lesions and bilateral anterior temporal subcortical cysts
Because of this imaging overlap, a key diagnostic step is to exclude congenital cytomegalovirus, including testing of stored neonatal blood spots where available
Children usually present in infancy with psychomotor delay, hypotonia and often seizures, and sensorineural hearing loss may be present
The clinical course is frequently non-progressive or only slowly progressive, distinguishing it from many other leukodystrophies
Diagnosis rests on the characteristic imaging combined with exclusion of congenital infection and confirmation of biallelic RNASET2 variants
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, with seizure control, developmental support, hearing rehabilitation and physiotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: This leukoencephalopathy is caused by biallelic loss-of-function variants in RNASET2, which encodes a ribonuclease of the transferase T2 family that participates in RNA turnover and lysosomal RNA degradation. Loss of enzyme activity is thought to disturb RNA processing and clearance, with downstream effects on neuroinflammation and glial function during early brain development. The resulting injury produces the distinctive combination of multifocal white matter abnormality and anterior temporal cysts, a pattern that strikingly resembles the sequelae of intrauterine cytomegalovirus infection despite the genetic cause.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital cytomegalovirus infection and other congenital (TORCH) infections
Vanishing white matter disease and other cystic leukoencephalopathies
Congenital muscular dystrophies with brain malformation and white matter change
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI to demonstrate multifocal white matter lesions with bilateral anterior temporal cysts
Congenital cytomegalovirus testing, including PCR of stored neonatal blood spots where possible
RNASET2 sequencing, with leukodystrophy panel or exome if targeted testing is negative
Audiometry for associated sensorineural hearing loss
Developmental assessment to guide supportive intervention
redFlags: Poorly controlled seizures or status epilepticus
Unexpected neurological regression prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
Progressive hearing loss impairing communication and development
reference.prognosis: The disorder is often static or only slowly progressive, with fixed motor and cognitive impairment of variable severity and, in many children, associated epilepsy and hearing loss; because it is largely non-progressive, prognosis relates mainly to the initial extent of brain injury and the burden of seizures rather than to ongoing degeneration.
pitfalls: Diagnosing congenital cytomegalovirus purely on imaging without genetic testing, or vice versa, given their close resemblance
Overlooking the anterior temporal cysts as a specific pattern clue
Assuming a progressive leukodystrophy and giving an unduly pessimistic prognosis for what is often a static condition
Failing to test stored neonatal blood spots when congenital infection needs to be excluded
Not arranging hearing assessment and developmental support
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: Provide supportive, symptomatic care as there is no disease-specific therapy for this ribonuclease deficiency
Control seizures with antiepileptic drugs and manage epilepsy where present
Address sensorineural hearing loss with audiological assessment and hearing aids or cochlear implantation as indicated
Support psychomotor delay and hypotonia with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy
Exclude congenital cytomegalovirus infection, whose imaging closely mimics this disorder, before attributing findings to the genetic cause
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive RNASET2-related condition and testing of at-risk relatives
Coordinate neurology and developmental paediatrics for long-term multidisciplinary follow-up
